what: The Bill Splitter divides shared costs fairly for trips, dinners, shared houses and events. For each expense you choose who paid and who shared it, and the tool works out how much each person owes or is owed.
It then suggests the fewest payments to settle everyone, so a group of six does not need fifteen transfers. Copy the summary or share it straight to WhatsApp.
uses: Track hotels, fuel and meals paid by different people.
Split a dinner, even when not everyone had the same.
Share costs for gifts or celebrations.
Keep track of who paid for what.
tutorial: Pick it from the list and optionally name the event.
Type a name and press Add. You can add several at once separated by commas.
Type what it was for and the amount, and choose who paid.
Everyone is ticked by default. Untick anyone who did not share that cost.
Press + Add expense for each cost.
Read “Who pays whom” for the payments, and check the balances table. Press Share on WhatsApp or Copy summary.
features: A smart settle-up plan instead of everyone paying everyone.
Choose exactly who shared each cost.
Splits never lose or add a cent.
Paid, share and balance for each person.
Send the summary to the group in one tap.
Keep adding expenses during a trip.

example.title: Worked example: a weekend trip
example.text: Ana pays 400 for the hotel shared by Ana, Ben, Chen and Dee (100 each). Ben pays 100 for a dinner shared by Ana, Ben and Chen (33.33 or 33.34 each). Chen pays 10 for a taxi shared by all four (2.50 each). The total is 510. The plan is: Chen pays Ana 125.83, Dee pays Ana 102.50 and Ben pays Ana 35.83, just three payments.

tips: Add expenses as they happen so nothing is forgotten.
Use one currency per split; convert foreign costs first with the Currency Converter.
Share the summary before anyone pays so everyone agrees.
Press Start over after settling to begin a new trip.
problems: It says to choose who paid
Every expense with an amount needs a payer.
It says to tick at least one person
Each expense must be shared by someone.
Someone pays a person they did not share with
That is normal: the plan minimises the number of payments, and everyone still ends up even.
